title: Forming a jazz group with Bill Williams and running a cabaret
summary: Bill Williams and his wife, with Bushell, formed a jazz group, then Williams leased a cabaret with five thousand dollars to start, though Puerto Ricans barely accepted jazz.

story.theme_name: Coming to New York: clubs, jams, and making it
story.community_name: Making it in New York: arrival, clubs and the scene

So I did that for another couple years or so. And I met a trumbone player who was a jazz man from L.A., but he was making his living down there selling encyclopedias. Got rich. And also was a good jazz man. He couldn't read music but he could play. Very big guy -- Bob Smiten. So he introduced me to another fellow who I found out later on was president of Williams International which was the largest printing company in Puerto Rico, and he was also a frustrated pianist. So, he suggested why don't don't we organize a group and play, you know, get together for kicks and may be we can book something and keep going. Well, his wife was also a drummer. She wanted to be a drummer. She used to be a ballerina at the Roxy Theater before she married Williams in New York, and they'd been living in Puerto Rico for, then, when I first arrived, they'd been living there for 20 years. They had a large family and all. So, we organized this group with his wife playing drums and him playing piano, and we picked up a trumpet player, an old retired Army man from Texas playing trumbone, and we got this jazz band. And we played service clubs -- we played for the Navy, we played for the Air Force, and this Bill Williams, he wouldn't take any money and neither would his wife, so if the gig paid, say, $40.00 a piece, they gave me their $80.00 and with my $40.00 I had $120.00 for a gig.

And sometimes I'd make $150.00 a gig for myself. So, to me it was a good business. And I took on a few pupils too. Private teaching wasn't much because Puerto Ricans weren't in the habit of paying $10.00 a lesson or something.. They could go to the conservatory for a whole season for -- whole semester for $25.00 -- all year. Attend the conservatory -- $25.00. That's all it cost. Government subsidizes the rest of it, I think, through the Ford Foundation and some other benevolent society. And we kept on with this thing until Bill said, "I got another idea." Down in the candata -- that's down there where the Americans are, down the strip, "Why don't we get a cabaret?" I said, "Well, you can get a cabaret, I don't have --" He said, "Don't worry about that, I'll get a place." Well, that man had so much confidence in me and enjoyed it so much, he went out and bought a cabaret -- leased it, rather, and put $5,000.00 in my hands and said, "Now, here's your expense account, now put your band in." So, I got some other musicians and I replaced them with a drummer -- had a good drummer there, and also a piano player, Gene Gilbo, who was piano player with the Trainiers, from California. Most of them were stationed here. He'd been with them for 25 years.
